description: How DVD kiosks and rental stores imploded while streaming platforms exploded — a chart-race from 2000→2026 showing Blockbuster's collapse vs the streaming giants that replaced it.
youtube_description:
0:00 Intro — The Rental Graveyard
0:18 2000–2006: Blockbuster at its peak (9,000+ stores)
0:50 2007: Netflix launches streaming — first pivot
1:20 2008–2012: Redbox and DVD kiosks surge, then top out
1:50 2010: Blockbuster files Chapter 11 (real turning point)
2:20 2013–2016: Netflix originals (House of Cards) accelerate subscriber growth
2:55 2018–2020: Streaming consolidates; Hulu, Prime scale up
3:30 2021–2026: The final extinction of rental footprints; streaming dominance
4:00 Sources & methodology

Watch this as a chart-race: a physical industry collapsing into a digital one. The dataset tracks Blockbuster store counts (thousands) vs streaming subscribers (millions) and Redbox kiosks from 2000–2026. Key milestones called out: Blockbuster's bankruptcy (2010), Redbox peak kiosk rollout (~2009–2011), Netflix global expansion and Originals push (2013+), Hulu & Prime's growth and the pandemic acceleration of streaming (2020).

Sources: Netflix annual reports and shareholder letters, Blockbuster bankruptcy filings and historic store-count reporting, Redbox corporate filings and press releases, Disney/Hulu investor releases, Amazon investor relations, industry coverage from The New York Times, Variety, The Wall Street Journal, Statista and historical business press. (Specific links used during research are: Netflix Investor Reports (2008–2023), Blockbuster 2010 bankruptcy coverage — NYT, Deadspin, Redbox SEC/press releases, Disney investor presentations.)

If you want the raw CSV or sources pinned in the thread, comment below and I’ll drop links. Subscribe for weekly chart-race videos and hit the bell if you want a breakdown of how we normalized store counts vs subscriber numbers for visuals.

instagram_caption:
🎬 From aisles of DVDs to endless autoplay: the 2000→2026 collapse you can’t unsee.

Ten years ago Blockbuster still felt like forever — 9,000+ stores, neon signs, weekend crowds. Then 2007 quietly flipped the script: Netflix launched streaming and began a slow, relentless pull. By 2010 Blockbuster filed Chapter 11. That was the inflection point. Over the next decade thousands of storefronts vanished; by the late 2010s only a handful of franchise locations remained (today effectively one iconic store survives as a tourist relic).

Meanwhile a handful of digital platforms went from experiments to empires. Netflix: from under a million customers in the early 2000s to well over 200 million paid subscribers by the 2020s after Originals (House of Cards, 2013) and global rollouts. Redbox popped up as a physical middle ground — cheap kiosks at grocery stores — peaking around ~42,000 kiosks in the 2008–2011 window before declining as streaming erased even that niche. Hulu launched in 2008 and slowly built paid subscribers through bundled deals and content; Amazon used Prime as the Trojan horse to add video on top of shopping — Prime members now number in the hundreds of millions.

The numbers tell the drama: a giant built for blockbusters dies as nimble, subscription-first platforms cannibalize not just rentals but attention itself. Physical inventory, late-fee revenue, and weekend lines gave way to global catalogs and algorithmic recommendations.

Which moment surprised you most — Redbox’s sudden saturation, Blockbuster’s bankruptcy, or Netflix’s Originals gamble? Tell me which company you thought would survive and why. Drop your oldest Blockbuster memory or the first streaming show that hooked you.
